numbers.label: Emergency: police, fire, ambulance, search and rescue
numbers.why: Call first for any emergency. Police start a search.

numbers.label: Conservation Officer Service RAPP (Report All Poachers and Polluters): aggressive bear or cougar, attack, poaching
numbers.why: Toll free in BC, open 24/7 for conflicts that threaten public safety.

numbers.label: Satellite phone (cannot dial 911): emergency coordination number
numbers.why: A search preview gave a number for satellite phones. Not confirmed on an official page. VERIFY before you rely on it.

dispatch.t: Say: "I need help in the bush." Then your location first.
dispatch.n: E-Comm says the first operator confirms your location first.

dispatch.t: Read your latitude and longitude from this screen, slowly, digit by digit.
What happened, how many people, who is hurt and how.
Your phone number. Then stay on the line and answer the questions.
Save battery: screen dim, no games. Stay where you are unless told to move.

nosignal.t: No signal: try 911 anyway. It can use any carrier's tower in range.
iPhone 14 or later: Emergency SOS via satellite works in Canada (iOS 16.1 or later).
Satellite messenger such as an inReach: press SOS. It needs an active plan.
911 does not reach everywhere in BC.

stop.t: Sit down. Do not keep walking.
Where did you last know where you were?
Map, compass, GPS, sun, creeks, roads.
Stay put, or move only if sure. Doubt means stay.

stopMore.t: Staying put shrinks the area searchers must cover.
Signal in threes: 3 whistle blasts, 3 horn blasts, 3 fires.
Keep the phone in an inside pocket. Cold kills batteries.

bleed.t: Make it safe: unload guns. Call 911 or SOS.
Find the source. Press hard with both hands, arms locked.
Deep wound in groin or armpit: pack it with gauze, press at least 3 minutes.
Arm or leg bleed that pressure cannot stop: tourniquet above the wound, tight. Write the time.
Do not pack wounds of the chest or belly.

hypo.t: Early: stumbles, mumbles, fumbles, grumbles. Strong shivering.
Shivering slows or stops, drowsy: this is an emergency. Call.
Shelter, off the cold ground, dry layers, heat to the trunk first.
Mild and alert: warm sweet drink and food. Drowsy: nothing by mouth, keep flat, gentle.

intro.t: Leave a trip plan with someone you trust: who, where, when back.
Overdue: your contact calls 911 straight away and says you left a trip plan.
Tell them not to be afraid to call. A false alarm is better than a late search.
AdventureSmart also has its own online trip plan at adventuresmart.ca.

gear: Extra warm layer and rain shell

gearSrc.t: Based on AdventureSmart's 10 essentials plus hunter extras (Tip).

legal.t: Big game and upland birds: legal light ends 1 hour after sunset.
Ducks and geese: legal light ends half an hour after sunset.

tips: Turn around at sunset minus your walk out time and you reach the truck in daylight (Tip).
Hunting until legal light ends means walking out in the dark. Headlamp, known route, partner told (Tip).
Add extra time if you may pack meat. A loaded pack walks at half speed or less (Tip).
ios: This screen counts down and alerts you while it is open on the screen.
iPhone pauses web apps in the background and when the screen locks. The alert may not ring then.
Notifications from web apps need iOS 16.4 or later and the app added to the Home Screen, and even then a timer cannot always wake it.
So: also set an alarm in the iPhone Clock app. It always rings.

first.t: Never run from a bear or a cougar.
Bear spray on your chest or hip, never in the pack.

id.t: Grizzly: big shoulder hump, dished face, short round ears.
Black bear: no hump, straight face, taller ears.
Colour fools people. Black bears come brown and cinnamon too.
Grizzlies evolved in open country and tend to charge. Black bears more often flee to cover.

see.t: Leave quietly the way you came. Keep watching it.
Speak softly, back away slowly. If it leaves, do not follow.

see.h: Bear agitated: jaw popping, woofing, stomping, bluff charge
see.t: Speak calmly, back away slowly. No direct eye contact, keep it in sight. Spray out.
Yield slowly. Still coming: it may be predatory. Yell, get to higher ground, spray, be ready to fight.

steps: Knocked down: lie on your stomach.
Hands clasped over the back of your head and neck. Feet slightly apart. Keep your pack on.
Stay still until you are sure it has left.
contact.note: Same for black bear and grizzly. Keep your pack on is a Tip.

contact.h: Predatory attack (stalks you, keeps coming, comes at night, the attack does not stop)
steps: Fight back with everything you have.
Hit the face, eyes and nose.
contact.note: Rare. Black bears may show predatory behaviour more often than grizzlies (WildSafeBC).

cougar.t: Stay calm. Never run. Never turn your back.
Look as large as possible. Keep it in view.
Back away slowly. Leave it a clear exit.
It follows or acts aggressive: be aggressive back. Eye contact, yell, loud noise.
Attacked: always fight back. Never play dead. Face and eyes. Use spray.

spray.t: In a holster on your chest or hip, dominant hand side. Practise the draw in gloves.
Bear within about 5 to 10 m (16 to 33 ft) and coming. It is a last resort tool.
spray.n: WildSafeBC: 5 to 10 m. Parks Canada: the can reaches about 10 m, effective range about 5 m.

spray.t: Pull the safety clip. Nozzle pointed away from you.
At the bear's face, slightly down, so the cloud forms a wall between you.
Short bursts of 1 to 2 seconds until the bear turns away. Keep some in reserve.
spray.n: Parks Canada's page says one second bursts, its video says two seconds; Alberta says 1 to 2 seconds.

spray.t: Wind or rain weakens it. Strong wind in your face: it will hit you. Stay out of the cloud's path.
Leave the area right away, watching the bear. Report it.

sprayMore.t: Alberta by distance: 9 to 15 m a short warning blast; under 9 m bursts of 1 to 2 seconds aimed slightly down in front of the head.
Cold weakens spray pressure. On frozen mornings keep it inside your jacket (Tip).
In the truck: safety clip on, in a sealed container or the trunk. Avoid heat and cold extremes.

report.t: Report aggressive bears or cougars, attacks and kill sites near people to the RAPP line.

rules.t: 15 cm: one person walking or skating alone.
20 cm: a group, skating parties or games.
These numbers are for clear blue ice, the strongest kind. White or grey ice is weaker.
Thickness changes across a lake. Springs, currents and inflows thin it. Check more than one spot.

tips: October and November ice is new. Most potholes will not reach 15 cm until well into winter (Tip).
Ducks on open water mean the ice near them is thin. Never walk out for a downed bird on new ice (Tip).

rules.t: Avalanches can happen wherever there is snow on a steep slope, even before daily forecasts start.
2026 season: Avalanche Canada says daily forecasts begin 25 November at 4 PM.
rules.n: From Avalanche Canada's early season message, read 2026-10-16.

rules.t: Past seasons started 22 to 25 November. Forecasts usually end in spring: VERIFY the end date each year.
Steep snow: transceiver, probe and shovel, and the training to use them.

tips: Strong gusts drop dead trees. Stay out of burned or beetle killed timber in a wind (Tip).
Freezing level near your hunting height: rain turns to snow up there. Pack for both (Tip).
Wet and windy at about 0 to 10 degrees is prime hypothermia weather (Tip).
